https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/18/russ.text: Russians began voting Friday in a tightly controlled three-day election that will likely see President Vladimir Putin tighten his grip on power after 26 years at the helm, as Russia's all-out war in Ukraine continues well into its fifth year.Only parties backing Putin and his war in Ukraine are on the ballot: the ruling United Russia, the Communist Party, A Just Russia, the nationalist LDPR and New People.Yabloko, Russia's only publicly anti-war party still operating inside the country, was barred from participating. The party saw a surge in social media support, particularly among young people, after it was initially allowed to stand.An unnamed European diplomat said the elections were "pretty much a sham" but described them as "a ritual the Kremlin considers necessary," adding that it would seek to ensure a high turnout.Independent observers have previously documented the use of state resources to influence results, including bussing voters to polling stations, pressuring employees of state institutions to vote for the ruling party, and pushing online voting as it is easier to monitor and control."As in the Soviet era, elections must demonstrate the loyalty of citizens," Russian political scientist and Head of Analysis of Transformation Processes at the NEST Centre Nikolai Petrov said.The election will fill 450 State Duma seats and the governorships of 11 federal regions, with the country's only remaining anti-war party excluded from the ballot and fears of mobilisation overshadowing the vote.Running from 18 to 20 September, the election will also choose deputies to regional legislatures in 39 federal subjects.Voters will choose eight of the 11 regional heads directly, while regional parliaments will elect the remaining three. Polling stations have been opened at Russian border crossings with Poland and the three Baltic states.Half of the 450 Duma seats will be allocated through nationwide party lists and the other half through single-member constituencies.Voting in Russian elections is also taking place in parts of Ukraine occupied by Moscow's troops, a move that neither Kyiv nor the West recognises as legitimate.Kremlin pushes pro-army narrativeAlmost 200 candidates in these elections have taken part in Russia's war in Ukraine, according to electoral commissions.The Kremlin has promoted them as part of Russia's "true elite," but the initiative is primarily a recruitment tool to boost Moscow's troops on the front lines, with few standing any real chance of being elected.Ahead of the vote, Putin urged Russians to vote to show troops that "behind our fighters stand millions of people" and to deliver an "answer to those who want to weaken Russia".Meanwhile, Russians fear another wave of military mobilisation, despite Putin personally denying plans for a call-up twice in three days in September alone.Independent Russian media have counted 17 official denials of an imminent mobilisation. Russia called up 300,000 reservists in the autumn of 2022 in a move that triggered significant public alarm and a mass departure of men of fighting age from the country.Tatiana Stanovaya of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre, which is banned in Russia, said she considered a new draft unlikely."They have put so much effort into persuading Russians not to worry about this," she said. "I would be very, very surprised if it happened."In the streets of Moscow today, few visible signs indicate an election is even under way.Fears of mobilisation have been further compounded by Ukrainian long-range drone strikes on Russian infrastructure in a bid to defund its war machine, causing fuel shortages and economic losses running into billions of euros.Many Russians feel the attacks break what Stanovaya described as the Kremlin's tacit bargain with the population over the war.In prison, in exile, deadAll of Putin's main political opponents are in prison, in exile or dead. Alexei Navalny, his most prominent challenger, died in a Russian penal colony in 2024.Putin's political opponents have mostly been driven into exile and his main opponent Alexei Navalny died in an Arctic prison in 2024.Russia's exiled opposition has urged anti-Kremlin Russians not to boycott the elections but instead vote "against Putin's party".Navalny's widow Yulia Navalnaya also called on anti-war Russians to cast their ballots at noon on Sunday.Yabloko — which critics say outlived its usefulness after the Kremlin allowed it to exist for many years to create a pretence of political plurality as a catch-all for liberal and discontented voters — disagreed, arguing that it was better not to vote."You are suggesting that we once again go, like sheep, dancing to their tune, and vote for those who have caused the deaths of people in Russia and Ukraine?" party chairman Nikolay Rybakov said this week.'Mad printer'Parliamentary elections were previously a source of significant political tension: in 2011, mass fraud during the Duma vote and Putin's return to the presidency from the post of prime minister triggered the largest street protests in Russia since the collapse of the Soviet Union.Putin has ruled Russia since 1999 and his United Russia party has dominated politics since the early 2000s.Under Putin, the Duma's powers have been substantially curtailed, reducing it largely to approving legislation initiated by the Kremlin — a role that has earned it the popular nickname "the mad printer" to mock the speed at which it rubber-stamped highly restrictive and controversial laws.Any criticism of the war is treated under Russian law as "discrediting the army" and can carry a prison sentence.Older voters remain among Putin's strongest supporters, although many still complain about living standards.

https://www.dw.com/en/israel-orders-home.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OZpc The attack took place at a checkpoint at the entrance of the West Bank city of Hebron Image: Mahmoud Illean/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Israeli Prime Benjamin Netanyahu ordered a massive operation in the West Bank, saying his country would "act to destroy this place" after gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in the West Bank city of Hebron on Friday morning. Netanyahu said Israeli forces would enter the attackers' neighborhood and displace its residents. "We will evacuate the residents, we will go from house to house, we will also seize the weapons there, and all the terrorist infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed," Netanyahu said, according to his office. The Israeli military said it killed the two attackers. In addition to the two Israeli soldiers killed, three more were lightly wounded in the attack that took place at a temporary military checkpoint at the entrance to Hebron on Friday. The deadly shooting in Hebron comes four days before Israeli elections on October 27, the first to take place since the Hamas attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023. Israeli army says 'terror attack' prevented after shooting To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The deadly shooting in West Bank: What to know The Israeli far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for a military campaign in the West Bank, "exactly like in Gaza," in response to Friday's incident. "There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign in Judea and Samaria to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons and eliminate terrorists. Exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon," Smotrich said, using the Israeli term for the West Bank. He said he called for the demolition of buildings near the site of Friday's shooting. "Following the attack, I have ordered the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site," he said. "The order will be carried out within the next hour and will take place throughout the afternoon hours." Smotrich, himself a settler in the West Bank, is widely known for championing ultranationalist and inflammatory policies. He has previously made similar calls for "war" in the West Bank. How much power do Israeli settlers have over West Bank policy? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Netanyahu ordered closure of West Bank after Friday's shooting incident Netanyahu said in an earlier statement on X that he had instructed the military to "impose a cordon on the city of Hebron and to prepare for a full closure of the entire West Bank starting today." There was not much known about the Israeli operation in the West Bank at that time. Israel has steadily tightened its grip in the occupied West Bank, having built dozens of outposts, considered illegal under international law, in the territory over the years. Settler violence has been on the rise in the West Bank , which Israel occupied during the 1967 Six-Day War, with dozens of Palestinians having been killed since the start of the year. Israeli elections take place next week: What to know The incident comes at a critical time for Israel. The Israeli election on October 27 is widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving prime minister, who has been criticized by opponents for failing to prevent the Hamas attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023. Polls indicate that the elections will be a close race between the pro- and anti-Netanyahu blocs. Israel elections: Who is Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's challenger? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Despite international attention on Gaza and the West Bank, there is little difference between the two blocs regarding Israel's treatment of Palestinians. Just days ago, masked Israeli settlers attacked a group of European diplomats and journalists in the West Bank as they accompanied Palestinians for the start of the annual olive harvest. The IDF condemned the acts of violence and opened a rare investigation into the settlers. Both Israel's occupation and the settlements, which are dotted throughout the territory, are illegal under international law. https://hotnews.ro/nicusor-dan-s-a-mutat.text: Președintele Nicușor Dan a anunțat că începând cu luna octombrie s-a mutat, împreună cu familia, într-o locuință de protocol. Șeful statului a fost întrebat, în conferința de marți seară de la Palatul Cotroceni, cât „au venit” facturile la curentul electric și la gaze. „Începând cu luna octombrie m-am mutat într-o locuință de protocol. Nu știu dacă am voie să vă spun unde”, a răspuns președintele, referindu-se la motive de securitate. El a precizat că, până la momentul mutării în locuința de protocol, „soţia” lui a fost cea care a achitat facturile: „Soția, evident”. La insistența presei privind cuantumul facturilor, Nicușor Dan a spus: „De ordinul 800-1.000 de lei. Pe câte două luni veneau”. Ulterior, șeful statului a fost întrebat dacă s-a căsătorit, având în vedere că s-a referit la partenera lui de viață, Mirabela Grădinaru, drept „soția”. „Încă nu, dar cred că pentru limbajul curent merge”, a adăugat președintele. După ce și-a preluat mandatul anul trecut în luna mai, Nicușor Dan a ales să rămână în locuința în care stătea înainte de a câștiga scrutinul prezidențială, alături de Mirabela Grădinaru și de cei doi copii ai lor.
